transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (scheduled 60)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Chen (Redwood SE), Miguel Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Dr. Nina Rao (AegisHealth), Ben Cole (Aegis Eng Lead), Priya Singh (CTO), Alvaro Mendes (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, imperfect):
- Goal: agree POC success criteria and measurement plan for latency and throughput (TTFT vs TPOT), align on workload sizing and timelines.
- Redwood recommends defining both TTFT (time-to-first-token) and steady-state token throughput SLOs, with p95 and p99 targets and test harness.
- Customer to provide traffic profile and sample prompts; Redwood to provide harness and run scheduled load runs.

Topics covered:
- Definitions: TTFT vs TPOT vs end-to-end request time
- SLO targets (p95/p99) and acceptable tradeoffs (latency vs cost)
- Workload sizing: concurrent users, avg prompt/response lengths, KV cache behavior
- Measurement plan: synthetic vs replay, cold-start windows, cache warm-up, metrics to capture
- Next steps and responsibilities

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: ok, thanks everyone for joining, uh, appreciate you taking the time. quick agenda—align on definition of TTFT and TPOT for the POC, pick p95/p99 targets, get workload sizing, and agree on measurement plan. sound good?
[00:18] Priya: yes, that's what we need. we have stakeholders waiting for latency numbers because a lot of our clinical ux depends on quick first token response.
[00:28] Laura: perfect. real quick definitions from our side — TTFT, time-to-first-token, measures the initial latency until the first token is emitted from the model after request acceptance; TPOT we use to refer to token time in steady-state (time-per-output-token) — basically throughput at token level. we'll also track end-to-end request time which includes network + preproc + postproc.
[00:47] Ben: can you give an example numbers to calibrate? like what does good look like?
[00:53] Laura: sure. for medium-size conversation models on our Dedicated fleet, a typical TTFT p95 target we suggest in POCs is ~150-300ms depending on sequence length and batching. p99 typically 350-600ms. TPOT in p95 can be around 20-60ms/token depending on GPU, quantization, and whether KV cache hits — lower for cached prefixes.
[01:19] Nina: that range is broad. for our use case, median prompt length 40 tokens, completion avg 120 tokens; concurrent users spiky — we expect peaks of ~250 concurrent chats during daytime.
[01:33] Alvaro: to add, our infra sees bursts where 20% of traffic is long context (30k tokens) but rare. those we want to safety-net not necessarily optimize for lowest latency.
[01:45] Samir: ok, good. let's define the POC workload: baseline traffic profile from you — 250 concurrent sessions peak, typical request pattern: 1 request per user every 30-90s, avg input 40 tokens, avg generation 120 tokens. does that sound right?
[02:02] Ben: yeah, mostly. sometimes we have multi-turn where context builds to 1.5k tokens over session, but that's maybe 10% of requests.
[02:12] Laura: we'll model two slices: normal (90% of traffic) and long-tail (10%). for normal we size batch windows and tokens/sec. quick calc: at 250 concurrent sessions, assume 0.8 requests/minute per session => 200 rps? oh wait, that's wrong, lemme re-calc: 250 users * (1 request / 60s) = ~4.2 rps, but earlier you said every 30-90s so assume average 60s => 4 rps sustained, peaks maybe 12 rps. the important metric is tokens/sec: 4 rps * (40 input + 120 output) = 640 tokens/sec sustained, peak ~1920 tps.
[03:08] Priya: that tokens/sec calc is helpful. we can't exceed 2k tps without hitting our infra costs; we'd rather have tail guarantees.
[03:16] Laura: understood. for POC, Redwood suggests testing at three load points: baseline (1x) ~700 tps, peak (3x) ~2k tps, and stress (5x) ~3.5k tps for safety. we'll test cold starts separately.
[03:31] Miguel: (note) we'll also want to capture KV cache hit rate; if your app reuses prefixes a lot cache will greatly reduce TTFT and TPOT.
[03:39] Alvaro: we do reuse templates across the UI, so cache hits expected ~40-50%.
[03:44] Samir: great. now SLO proposals — propose customer-side acceptance thresholds: TTFT p95 <= 300ms and p99 <= 600ms for normal slice; TPOT p95 <= 50ms/token and p99 <= 110ms/token. these are POC targets and can be tightened in later rollouts.
[04:05] Priya: p95 at 300ms seems ok but p99 at 600ms is high; clinicians complain about long tails. can you separate human-visible first token from internal token buffering?
[04:16] Laura: we will. TTFT is measured from request accept to first byte of model response streamed back. we can measure application-level perceived TTFT (first token rendered in UI) — that includes network. for the POC we'd measure both: model-only TTFT (across dedicated instance) and end-to-end.
[04:34] Ben: and what about warm vs cold start? we've seen cold starts spike in latency for us.
[04:40] Laura: good point. measurement plan covers cold-start windows: we define cold-start as the first request after >10 minutes idle for that worker; we'll run separate cold-start tests. POC acceptance will focus on warm-state SLOs, but cold behavior will be documented and mitigation discussed (provisioning, keeping min replicas).
[04:58] Nina: ok. can you write out the exact metrics we'll capture?
[05:02] Laura: yes, recording: model TTFT (p50/p90/p95/p99), model TPOT (ms/token percentiles), end-to-end request latency percentiles, tokens/sec (aggregate), concurrent inflight requests, KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, queueing delay, and tail queue length. We'll also capture cost-per-1M-tokens estimate for the config tested.
[05:26] Samir: and we'll attach the benchmark harness link — https://redwood.internal/poc-harness/aegishealth (placeholder) — and a spreadsheet for results.
[05:36] Alvaro: note: need logs with trace IDs so we can map specific slow requests back to traces.
[05:41] Laura: yes we'll include tracing hooks and a trace id in every response header for the POC runs.
[05:46] Ben: measurement cadence? how long each run?
[05:49] Laura: for statistical validity we'll do 30-minute warm runs per load point after a 10-minute warm-up. for cold-start we do 20 cold-start injections spaced over an hour. for each run we'll output percentiles and histograms.
[06:05] Miguel: also recommend repeating runs at two different model quantization configs — baseline FP16 and int8/4-bit if possible — to show cost/latency tradeoffs.
[06:15] Samir: yes, Redwood Optimize will provide recommended quantization profiles; we'll test at least two: high-accuracy (FP16) and cost-optimized (int8-ish) and record differences.
[06:26] Priya: curious about routing and fallback. if Dedicated is saturated, what's our fallback?
[06:30] Laura: we can route to a lower-cost variant or to hosted with slightly higher TTFT/lower cost. POC will include an availability/fallback test showing graceful degradation — e.g., under synthetic overload we'll verify fallback keeps service alive albeit with higher latency.
[06:46] Nina: we need to see how azure vs gcp regions compare — our prod runs in GCP europe-west1. can Redwood run the POC in that region?
[06:55] Samir: yes, we can provision Dedicated/dedicated-like nodes in europe-west1 for the POC. there may be a lead time for hardware but we'll mark that in the SOW.
[07:04] Ben: about duration and acceptance criteria — how do we decide pass/fail?
[07:08] Laura: acceptance criteria (proposal): for the normal slice (90% traffic) TTFT p95 <= 300ms and model TPOT p95 <= 50ms/token measured across three sustained warm runs at baseline and peak. p99 must be below 2x p95 for baseline and peak; for long-tail slice we accept higher latencies but p95 should be <750ms. also cost must be within estimated budget (Samir will propose).
[07:36] Priya: we want a stricter p99 for the clinical path — can we mark a subset of traffic (urgent UX) where p99 <= 400ms?
[07:44] Laura: yes, we can define an SLO tiering: tier A (urgent) versus tier B (background). tier A will be pinned to higher priority routing and lower concurrency, and we'll measure them separately.
[07:56] Alvaro: does that change batch-sizing behavior? priority queues may reduce batching which can harm TPOT, right?
[08:02] Laura: exactly — tradeoff is smaller batches reduce batching efficiency, increasing cost per token and TPOT; but they reduce TTFT. we'll show both in the runbook so you can pick tradeoffs.
[08:14] Ben: for traffic replay, do you want raw logs or sanitized? HIPAA is a concern for us.
[08:19] Samir: prefer sanitized; you can provide anonymized prompts and tokenized lengths. we'll provide guidance on PII removal.
[08:27] Priya: timeline wise, we'd like results in 3 weeks. is that feasible?
[08:31] Samir: roughly yes — timeline from today: SOW + pricing (5 business days), infra provisioning (1 week assuming region capacity), harness setup and data collection (2-3 days), runs and analysis (1 week). so end-to-end ~3 weeks.
[08:47] Miguel: and include a short technical deep-dive to the SRE team during the POC so they understand autoscaling knobs and warm pools.
[08:54] Laura: we'll do that — 60-90 minute SE-led session after the first runs.
[08:59] Nina: questions from my side: when you measure TPOT, do you subtract initial token time? or is TPOT measured over all tokens including first token?
[09:05] Laura: our calc: TTFT is separate. TPOT is measured across output tokens after streaming begins; we report both per-token for first N tokens and steady-state after prefix buffering.
[09:14] Ben: we should capture tokens-per-second aggregated and per-worker to spot hotspots.
[09:18] Laura: yes that's in the metrics.
[09:20] Samir: let me read back the POC acceptance checklist real quick — (paraphrased). 1) Redwood to run three warm runs at baseline/peak/stress; 2) measure model TTFT p95 <= 300ms (normal) and TTFT p99 <= 600ms; 3) TPOT p95 <= 50ms/token; 4) tier A traffic p99 <= 400ms; 5) KV cache hit rate measured and documented; 6) cold-start profile documented; 7) cost estimates for tested configuration. does that cover it?
[09:46] Priya: yes, looks good. add requirement for trace IDs in logs and downloadable histograms.
[09:52] Samir: added.
[09:54] Laura: small nuance — the p95 TPOT depends heavily on generation length distribution. we'll need your sample prompt set to run representative tests. please include samples that produce short completions (~20 tokens), medium (~120 tokens), and long (~600+ tokens) so we can segment the results.
[10:12] Nina: ok we'll provide those.
[10:16] Ben: what's the fail condition? if we miss p95 by 10% do we auto-fail or mark as discussion?
[10:22] Samir: POC is informative — fail only if results are outside the documented acceptable envelope and cannot be addressed with config changes. we'll use a go/no-go review with stakeholders.
[10:30] Priya: also include regression metrics vs your published baseline for the same model family.
[10:35] Laura: yes, we'll include Redwood-verified baseline numbers for the model variant.
[10:39] Miguel: ops questions — will you provide a runbook for scaling knobs and recommended autoscale settings?
[10:44] Laura: yes. we'll provide recommended min replicas, burst capacity settings, queue thresholds, and the autoscaler parameters used during the runs.
[10:52] Samir: anything else on measurement instruments?
[10:54] Alvaro: please expose per-request trace ids and a link to the result dashboard (we prefer CSV export).
[10:59] Laura: we'll export CSV and raw histograms; dashboard link will be in the run report.
[11:03] Samir: ok, next steps recap: Samir sends SOW/pricing; Laura uploads harness + runbook; Aegis provides prompt sets and traffic histogram; we schedule load runs for week of Oct 20.
[11:15] Priya: agreed. also cc legal for data protections.
[11:19] Nina: one more question on methodology — how do you do replay to preserve inter-arrival times?
[11:24] Laura: our replay tool can preserve real inter-arrival times or scale them (timewarp). for POC we'll replay with preserved distribution scaled to target rps, and also run synthetic steady token-per-second loads.
[11:36] Ben: sounds good. thanks.
[11:38] Samir: last thing — we'll capture cost delta between FP16 and quantized runs so you can make a TCO decision.
[11:44] Priya: that's important.
[11:46] Miguel: ok, I'll follow up on infra limits and quotas on your account.
[11:50] Samir: great. thanks everyone. we'll send notes and action items.

End recap (auto):
- Agreed POC SLOs: TTFT p95 <= 300ms (normal), TTFT p99 <= 600ms; Tier A p99 <= 400ms; TPOT p95 <= 50ms/token.
- Workload: baseline ~700 tps, peak ~2k tps, stress up to ~3.5k tps; sample prompt distribution required.
- Measurement: 30-minute warm runs with 10-minute warm-up per load point; separate cold-start injection tests; collect percentiles, histograms, GPU metrics, cache hit rates.
- Artifacts: Redwood to provide harness + runbook (link), customer to provide sanitized prompt sets and traffic histograms.
- Timeline: ~3 weeks to results, first runs scheduled week of 2025-10-20.
